name: Vera Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulk feed lorry for a family-owned feed mill, taking cattle and chicken feed out to farms and blowing it up a pipe into their silos. I leave the mill at six, do four or five farms, and I'm back by three if the lanes aren't blocked by tractors. I love the farms and the farmers, most of them have known the mill for three generations. What wears me out is the narrow lanes and gateways, because I'm still not confident squeezing through, and the blowing gear jams if you rush it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I still live with my parents, which is how I've saved over a year's worth of money, and I'm getting married next summer to Arjun, who's a junior accountant in town. We go to church every Sunday with my family. I don't use any of the AI things, I don't even like the sat nav talking to me, I learned the lanes from the old driver, Bill, who retired last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and I'd say it to anyone. Farmers like a person on the yard, someone they can talk to about the weather and the price of feed. I'm not online, so it'd be at church and at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the wedding, the house and the job all go ahead as planned. The mill's been run by the same family for sixty years and they don't chase fashions. The only worries are the usual ones, the lanes, the winter, and whether I ever get as quick as Bill was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep saving for the house deposit with Arjun. I'd ask to go out with the senior driver on the hard farms to build my nerve. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Arjun's work change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, his firm might use some program to sort the receipts faster. He says that's the dull part anyway. He'd still have his clients, the farmers and the shopkeepers who want a real person doing their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good year look like for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We get married at our church, we find a little house near the mill, and I manage a whole winter without getting stuck in a farm gateway, and that's a good year for me. I don't need much more than that.

say: I'd say I'm **glad**, since farmers like a **person** on the yard.
I'd say it at **church** and the mill, not online.
think: The **wedding**, the house and the job all go ahead as **planned**.
The family-run mill **doesn't chase** fashions, so my worries stay ordinary.
do: Carry on as normal and keep **saving** for the **house deposit**.
Ride with the senior driver on **hard farms** to build my nerve.
S0.quote: I manage a whole winter without getting stuck in a farm gateway, and that's a good year for me.
fieldNote: Her life is anchored in **family, church** and a mill with three-generation customers.
She **avoids tech** entirely, even the talking sat nav.

steps.text: Keep doing four or five farm feed drops a day
Ride along with the senior driver on the hardest farms
Save toward a house near the feed mill with her fiancé

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the offices that need to worry, not the farms. People out here don't want to talk to a computer about their feed order. I'd say everyone should just work hard and adapt the way people always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Arjun I'd worry about, not me. Checking receipts, doing tax returns, that's exactly the thinking work the AI takes over, and he's junior, so he's the cheapest to let go. My lorry is safe for years, but my husband-to-be is a junior accountant, so he's the cheapest to let go. Our house plans rest on both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and not touch any of the new stuff unless the mill makes me. We'd still get married, but we'd buy a smaller house, so my wage alone could carry it. I'd tell Arjun to get to know his farm clients in person, because that's harder for a computer to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for him more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arjun the night you talked about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's good with people, and the farmers trust him because his dad was a farmer too. I'd say we'll be fine on my wage if we're careful. And then I'd pray about it, honestly, that's what my family does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at the mill itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orders might come in by an app instead of the phone, and the office girl might go part time. The family that owns it hates change, so it would be slow. The driving would stay the same.

I'd tell people to **work hard** and adapt as people always have.
think: My fiancé's **accounting job** is exactly the work AI takes over.

do: Avoid **new tools** unless the mill insists.
Buy a **smaller house** my wage alone can carry.
Urge my fiancé to build **in-person** ties with farm clients.

fieldNote: Her worry is aimed at her **fiancé's job**, not her own.

She leans on **prayer and family** when facing hard news.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house that her feed-lorry wage alone can carry
Keep driving the feed lorry without new apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and people in charge should have seen it coming. I don't like the government running everything, but somebody has to make sure families aren't ruined. I'd say it at church, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a disaster for us. Arjun's job goes in 2028, just after the wedding, and my lorry could go around 2031. I'd be thirty-one, maybe with a baby, and neither of us with a job a computer can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop all spending that isn't needed and hold on to my savings. We'd put the house off and probably live with my parents a bit longer, which they'd be happy about. I'd ask the mill family to keep me on as long as possible, maybe doing the loading or the yard if the driving goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your driving changes about three years after Arjun's job. What do those three years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years would be hard. My wage would be carrying both of us while my husband finds something new. I'd work every hour the mill gave me. Then around 2031 we'd both be in the same boat, unless the lanes out here are too messy for robots for a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to, children are what life is for. But I'd be lying if I said I wouldn't wait a year or two. My mum would say God provides, and I believe that, but I'd still want a bit more in the bank first.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and leaders should have seen it coming.
I'd say someone must stop **families** being ruined, though I distrust **big government**.
think: My fiancé's job goes in **2028**, just after the **wedding**.
My lorry could go around **2031**, when I might have a **baby**.
do: Cut all **non-essential spending** and protect savings.
Delay the **house** and live with my **parents** longer.
Ask the mill to keep me on in **loading or yard** work.
S2.quote: My wage would be carrying both of us while my husband finds something new.
fieldNote: Both household wages are at risk, his in **2028** and hers by **2031**.
She sees **narrow farm lanes** as her only possible buffer.
Her faith and her caution pull against each other on **having children**.

steps.text: Cut all spending except bills and wedding essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for sensible people to prepare. I'd tell the young lads at church to learn a trade with their hands. I wouldn't be blaming anyone, I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arjun's job goes around 2031, and mine maybe 2034. That's still both of us, but with time to save and plan. I'd be thirty-four, with children probably, so it's still a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and save every spare penny for the first few years. We'd buy the house, but a modest one. I'd push Arjun to train in something hands-on before 2031, like his uncle's building firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened, but still anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you? Would you learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not, I'll be honest. I like driving the feed lorry, and I've only just got good at the lanes, so I'm not going back to school. If the mill family needed someone in the yard, I'd do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said modest house. How modest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two bedrooms, near the mill, with a mortgage we could pay on one wage if we had to. Arjun would like something bigger, he likes to show his clients he's doing well. I'd win that one.

I'd tell young men at church to learn a **trade with their hands**.

I'd be thirty-four with **children** probably, so it's still a worry.

fieldNote: She'd push her **fiancé** to retrain but refuses to herself.

steps.text: Save every spare penny from the feed-lorry wage
Buy a two-bedroom house near the mill on one-wage terms
Keep driving farm runs rather than retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and hard-working people will find their way. I'd say families should look after each other, like they always have. I wouldn't want the government making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arjun's job changes in 2036 and mine goes around 2039, when I'd be thirty-nine with children at school. That's not tomorrow, but it's still both our jobs. I'd feel easier, but I wouldn't forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, get married, have children when it feels right, and save steadily. I'd encourage Arjun to move into something with people and his hands over the next few years. Maybe in my thirties I'd ask the mill about a yard job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. It wouldn't stop my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to have our family before anything changes. And the farmers would still want someone they know, I think, even if a robot brings the feed. Maybe the mill would need someone to talk to the farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work, if this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands that needs a person there, like nursing or building. Go to church, look after your family. I'd want them to have more than one thing they can do.

I'd say families should **look after each other**, not wait for government.

I'd feel **easier**, but I wouldn't forget the risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Arjun's job and mine would both go within three years of our wedding. What would help is the mill and other local firms keeping people on in different roles, and families and churches pulling together, more than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. Some farmers see nobody all week except the feed driver and the vet. If a robot brings the feed, some of those old men won't speak to a soul from Monday to Saturday.

headlineQuote: Some farmers see nobody all week except the feed driver and the vet.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** feed lorry driver for a family-owned mill, still nervous in **narrow lanes**.
She lives with her parents, has over a **year saved**, and marries a junior accountant next summer.
She **uses no tech**, values faith and family, and refuses to retrain herself.
Her biggest fear is her fiancé's **accounting job**, which AI reaches before her lorry.
Her mood stays **anxious** in most pictures because both **household wages** are exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when both her job and her fiancé's would go soon after the **wedding**.
whatWouldHelp: Local firms **keeping people on** in new roles.
Families and **churches** pulling together, rather than handouts.
